cards.summary: The only support is one uncontrolled anecdote in Superpowers' own writing-skills guide (a 'code review between tasks' description led to one review instead of two). Anthropic's docs say descriptions should state both what the skill does and when to use it. No measured rate exists in either direction; measured activation studies only show that trigger phrasing ('Always invoke for...', unique anchor tokens) raises recall.

contrarian.claim: Description should include what the skill does AND when to use it; description is the discovery mechanism among 100+ skills
contrarian.modelEra: model-agnostic docs, applies to Claude 5 era
contrarian.note: Official guidance (opened and confirmed). It is guidance, not a measurement; it does not address the skip-the-body failure mode, and its own examples ('Extract text and tables from PDF files... Use when...') are what-plus-when, not workflow summaries. So the real conflict is narrower: capability summary vs step-by-step workflow summary.

contrarian.claim: Skill-trigger evaluation shows recall rises with an added trigger sentence and unique anchor tokens; says nothing about workflow summaries
contrarian.modelEra: one unnamed mid-tier frontier model via Claude Code SDK (2026)
contrarian.note: 951 positive prompts, 20 skills, one run per prompt: micro-recall 46.3% to 67.3% after adding 'Always invoke for...'. Supports trigger-oriented wording but explicitly does not test workflow-summary descriptions.

failures.what: Superpowers writing-skills: the sole cited evidence for the rule is one before/after observation, no sample size or repetitions
failures.whatItShows: Rule is plausible but unmeasured; a web search for a measured test found none.

failures.what: Superpowers issue #2423: emphatic always-invoke wording and the writing-skills guide's pressure register over-trigger on Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5
failures.whatItShows: Same source that taught the trigger-only rule is itself reported to over-trigger on Claude 5.5; no repro logs, no maintainer reply. Weak, but it shows the source's calibration is Claude-4-era.

conditions: Holds best where the description is the only thing the model sees before deciding to load, and the body contains multi-step procedure that a summary could be mistaken for.
Less relevant in a script-driven harness where scripts, not the model, decide which skill/packet runs: description-triggered discovery is not the path.
Capability summary ('extracts text from PDFs') is not the same as a workflow summary; Anthropic's recommendation only conflicts with the latter.
cards.conclusion: Treat as a cheap, plausible heuristic with n=1 evidence, not a finding. For a script-driven harness that injects skill bodies itself, the failure mode (model skips body after reading description) mostly does not arise, so the rule has low value there; keep descriptions to what+when per Anthropic but avoid embedding step lists. A 20-run A/B on Claude 5 models (workflow-summary vs trigger-only description, count of body steps completed) would settle it.

cards.summary: Anthropic's own skill guide prescribes evaluation-driven development with a no-skill baseline, and SkillsBench (curated skills +16 to +25pp, self-generated skills negative) shows skills must be validated, not assumed helpful. Superpowers' own recent PRs (Opus 5/5.5) show a baseline can reveal that a rule changes nothing, but I could not find the '0 placeholders in 60 plans' figure; what I found is a no-skill arm building the product 2/2 and a 4,200-line plan baseline.

contrarian.claim: Baseline comparison is cheap but small-n and can mislead: the Opus 5.5 ablation used 2 runs per arm, one fixture, and subagents inheriting the maintainer's CLAUDE.md
contrarian.note: Opened PRs: placeholder presence was never measured; the claimed '0 placeholders in 60 plans' figure was NOT found in #2333 or #2379. What is measured: building-during-planning 2/2 with rule removed and 2/2 with no skill, vs 0/5 with the rewrite. Shows the method works but with tiny n.

failures.what: SkillsBench: self-generated skills reduce pass rate (-1.3pp early version; -8 to -11.5pp later version); curated skills +16 to +25pp. Reported only via secondary summaries (alphaxiv/emergentmind), paper not directly opened
failures.whatItShows: Skills are not automatically helpful; baseline-vs-skill measurement is justified. Non-peer-reviewed, version numbers vary.

conditions: Needs enough runs: the one Claude 5.5 ablation had n=2 per arm, which cannot detect modest effects.
Pressure scenarios must be run on the target model generation; Claude 5 docs say older skills 'can degrade output quality' on Fable 5, so baselines must be re-run per model.
Baseline is most informative as a keep/delete test for a rule, not as proof the rule helps in the wild.
cards.conclusion: The method itself is sound and endorsed by Anthropic; no credible source argues against baseline comparison. The counter-example is a caution about sample size, and the specific '0 in 60' claim is unverified. On Claude 5-era models the likely finding is that many scaffolding rules are no-ops or harmful, which makes baselines more, not less, valuable. Verdict would drop if evidence showed baseline results fail to predict real-use behavior.

cards.summary: Concrete numbers beat vague adjectives for specification, but a number in a prompt is not enforcement: instruction-following research shows constraint violation grows with stacked constraints (Claude Sonnet 4.6 follow rate 96% down to 20% at 20+ constraints in one preprint), and Anthropic's Claude 5 docs steer toward explaining intent and softening MUST-style language. In a script-driven harness the right place for a count is the script's counter.

contrarian.claim: Instruction follow rate collapses non-linearly as stacked verifiable constraints accumulate, driven by pairwise conflicts
contrarian.note: Preprint with released verifiers; 24 instructions, rates ~96% to ~20%. Compression via prompt rewrite helps weaker models by up to 11pts, stronger barely change. Not a test of numeric limits specifically; mid-tier models.

contrarian.claim: Frontier ceiling for simultaneous instructions moved from ~200-300 to ~2,000; failures at scale shift to refusals, partial output
contrarian.modelEra: GPT 5.5, Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Pro
contrarian.note: Keyword-inclusion proxy task; vendor blog; shows that rule count per se is not the binding limit for 2026 frontier models at harness-realistic sizes (tens of rules).

contrarian.claim: Don't shout MUST/CRITICAL; Claude 4.5+ over-triggers on emphatic language; give the reason behind the instruction
contrarian.who: Anthropic (prompting best practices, incl. Fable 5 / Claude 5 pages)
contrarian.note: Opened and confirmed ('dial back aggressive language'; 'explaining why such behavior is important'). This is about emphasis, not numbers: 'max 3 loops' is not an adjective-style emphasis, so it does not contradict the card.

failures.what: Superpowers-style pressure/emphatic wording over-triggers on Opus 5.5 / Sonnet 5.5 (report only)
failures.whatItShows: Style of adjectives/emphasis is risky; says nothing about numeric limits.

failures.what: Search snippets claim tool-call-count limits are among the most violated constraints (CCTU benchmark 2603.15309) and word-count limits are frequently violated (2601.17789)
failures.whatItShows: NOT CONFIRMED: PDF fetch returned only metadata, so numbers could not be verified; treat as unverified pointer.

conditions: Holds for specifying scope/format/limits unambiguously ('at most 5 bullets', 'two review rounds').
A prompt-stated cap on loops/calls is advisory; enforce with a script counter. No study found testing a prompted iteration cap on Claude 5.
Fails when counts accumulate into many simultaneous constraints on weaker or smaller models; pair with explained rationale instead of capitals.
cards.conclusion: The claim is directionally right (precision beats vagueness) but over-sold if it implies models reliably honour numbers. For Claude 5-era models rule-count degradation is smaller than the 2025 literature suggests, yet no source tests prompted loop caps directly. In a script-driven harness, state the count AND enforce it in code; the Anthropic 'explain why' advice complements rather than contradicts it. A direct test of a stated '3 loops' cap on Claude 5.5 would change the verdict.

cards.summary: Anthropic itself publishes separate prompting pages per Claude model and says to re-check technique against your own evals before applying to another; it also says skills built for older models can degrade Fable 5. Cross-model prompt transfer research (PromptBridge 'model drifting') supports it, but evidence is mostly pre-2026 models and abstract-level, and maintenance cost is real.

contrarian.claim: Prompt-transfer degradation ('model drifting') is common and severe, so per-model prompts/tuning are needed
contrarian.note: Supports the card, not refutes. Abstract gives no numbers; only abstract was opened.

contrarian.claim: Over-tuned/scaffolded prompts become liabilities when models change; remove old instructions if defaults are better
contrarian.note: 'Skills developed for prior models are often too prescriptive ... and can degrade output quality.' Opened and confirmed. Supports a counter-cost: per-model prompts rot at each model release, so maintenance burden is real, and Anthropic's skill guide says to aim for instructions that work across Haiku/Sonnet/Opus.

failures.what: Anthropic skill guide: test with all models; 'aim for instructions that work well with all of them'
failures.whatItShows: Anthropic recommends one portable prompt tested across models rather than forks, while also publishing per-model guidance; the two are in tension.

conditions: Worth forking only when a model's measured behavior diverges (e.g. Opus 5 verbosity, Sonnet effort calibration, Haiku early stopping per Anthropic's per-model pages).
Within one family (Claude 5.x) a shared base prompt plus small per-model deltas is the cheaper pattern.
Cross-vendor (Claude vs GPT/Grok) forks are better supported than intra-family forks.
cards.conclusion: Per-model variants are justified by Anthropic's own per-model pages and by transfer research, but the gain is unmeasured for your harness and the cost is a re-tune at each release. Prefer a shared core with measured per-model deltas, each retired when an eval shows no difference. Evidence quality here is thin (abstract-level); a measured A/B of a shared vs forked prompt on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 would settle it.

cards.summary: Controlled studies find repository context files (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) do not generally improve task success and add 20%+ cost; LLM-written ones slightly hurt, human-written ones help only for non-standard practices. Curated skills do help (SkillsBench), self-generated ones do not. All context-file studies used pre-Claude-5 models.

contrarian.claim: Context files do not generally improve task success rates and raise cost by over 20%; repo overviews are unhelpful, useful only for non-standard practices
contrarian.modelEra: 2025 models/agents (SWE-bench style, Python); abstract only opened, secondary summaries give -2% LLM-generated / +4% human-written
contrarian.note: Abstract confirmed. Per-model numbers not verified from the full paper. Python-only, 138 tasks per secondary source.

contrarian.claim: Context-injection strategy (none/always-on/selective) did not measurably change correctness; effect bounded to <=10-15pp
contrarian.modelEra: claude-sonnet-4-6 and gpt-5.5 (closest to Claude 5 era found)
contrarian.note: 17 tasks, 3 repos, 288 runs; minimum detectable effect above 30pp, channels differ between agents. Underpowered, so 'no effect' is weak.

failures.what: SkillsBench: curated skills +16 to +25pp, self-generated skills negative or negligible
failures.whatItShows: Value depends on curation; secondary-source summary only.

failures.what: Anthropic: older skills/prompts too prescriptive for Fable 5 and can degrade output
failures.whatItShows: Instruction files may need pruning at each model generation.

conditions: Instruction files help for non-obvious conventions, test commands, and constraints the repo cannot show; they do not help as architecture overviews.
Always measure with and without on your own tasks (Anthropic's own recommendation).
Evidence on Claude 5.x agents with context files is absent in what I found.
cards.conclusion: Keep instruction files short and limited to non-inferable facts, and baseline them. The best studies predate or only touch Claude 5; absence of Claude 5.x evaluations is itself a finding. Instruction-following ceilings have risen (Arize: ~2,000 simple constraints for 2026 models), so rule count matters less than rule relevance.
